newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraqi dinar soars on oil-for-food deal news.
newsitem.headline: Iraqi dinar soars on oil-for-food deal news.

text.p: Iraq's dinar currency surged on Monday following news that Baghdad had agreed to all U.N. conditions blocking the implementation of an oil-for-food deal.
A statement was read over state radio and television which also broadcast national songs in jubilation.
The dinar, which earlier in the day traded at about 1,650 to the U.S. dollar, soared to nearly 1,100 and traders said further gains were expected on Tuesday.
However, few kerb dealers were seen at Kifah where money changes hands at rates higher than the government-licensed shops. Despite the drastic cut in the price of the dollar, there were few buyers.
Official exchange houses put up their shutters. "Until minutes ago I bought dollars at 1,650 dinars each. Business has become almost impossible," said one money changer.
Ordinary Iraqis had seen it all before and were sceptical.
"It has become a long story. I will only believe when I receive my share of food supplies from the deal," said a passer-by.
Iraqi U.N. Ambassador Nizar Hamdoon said Baghdad had agreed to all U.N. conditions that had held up the deal and predicted oil could start flowing in December.
The deal permits Iraq oil sales worth $2 billion in six months to allow it to purchase food and medicine, in short supply because of U.N. sanctions imposed after Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
The pact was signed in May but was put on hold when Baghdad sent troops into northern Iraq late in August in support of one Kurdish faction against another.
Shops were already closed in Baghdad when news spread that oil could flow soon. The impact on prices of essential commodities, in short supply in the Iraqi capital, was not immediately known.
One of the issues that has been obstructing the deal has been Iraqi insistence on controlling the number, make-up and freedom of movement of a U.N. team to observe its implementation on the ground.

"If the pricing formula is approved -- which we hope to get this week -- then nothing else remains," Hamdoon said. He was referring to action by the Security Council's Iraqi sanctions committee, which must approve a formula governing oil sales contracts.
